author: sky.cactus
content: Ideas being one's own isn't sufficient by itself.  You need to have ideas that are deemed sufficiently high value relative to volume.  If you post 3 essays a week on a range of topics and all of them don't pass the bar of "this is interesting and worthy of further consideration", then you are likely to get blocked for spam, regardless of whether you used an AI to write those essays or you wrote them yourself.

author: sky.cactus

I haven't dug through what you posted, but the moderators have to draw a line somewhere, and that line may catch humans in it (and likely will catch more and more humans as AIs get smarter and smarter).

author: chugartx
content:
<@592004585506340885> <@796570016966770688> <@845691100072509460> <@301186049323958275> <@365300888354422794> <@892053833121923094> "If two conforming implementations can disagree because of one sentence, the fork already exists conceptually. The code has only not manifested it yet."

That is what I’ve been trying to explain this whole time. I’m not asking anyone to trust me, accept every PR I make, or spend unlimited time reviewing me. But when the answer is “we can’t tell what you actually understand,” then ask me. Push on the claim. Make me defend it. I can be wrong. What I don’t think makes sense is turning “we don’t know” into a conclusion about what I’m capable of before that ever happens.

This ERC-8414 conversation is exactly what I mean: https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/erc-8414-token-bound-task-tenders/29597?u=chugarchugarr. I raised a distinction in the language, it was challenged against what the mechanism actually does, the author agreed the wording promised more than the design delivered, and the conversation moved forward. Now, after my part of the discussion, another precision problem of the same kind has surfaced and a downstream contributor checked the actual contract and realized their own wording inherited it. That is why I care so much about semantics. These aren’t word games. The words eventually become behavior.

You absolutely have the right to decide what deserves your review time. My concern is deciding who is worth listening to before testing what they’re actually saying. With AI making it cheaper and cheaper to produce code and proposals, that distinction is only going to matter more. Otherwise we can decentralize execution while quietly rebuilding privileged observers in the human layer that decides what ever gets done. Sounds like the EXACT system we are already in.

author: chugartx
content:
And fwiw, I don’t need my perspective to win. This isn't a game. This is real life. I need it to be allowed to fail for the right reason. If the claim is wrong, kill it. If it survives, inherit whatever survived. But don’t replace that process with an assumption about the person making it.

"If downstream implementations have to silently narrow a word to remain consistent with the machine, the specification was already carrying unresolved state."

This conversation is a test to what WILL happen in the future x1000. I just want to help with that problem.
